title: Worker pool
contract: Four workers consume a bounded queue; every input produces exactly one result, and completion closes the result stream.
checks: Empty input and forty jobs, with a uniqueness set, exact count, and independently expected sum.
gsharpNotes: Directional handles express what each stage can do. Nested scope joins the workers before the coordinator closes results.
goNotes: Channels and WaitGroup.Go express the same topology. A coordinator explicitly waits before closing results.
limits: Result order is unspecified. Queue capacity bounds buffered values, not worker count or total report memory.

title: Bounded concurrency
contract: Acquire admission before spawning work, keep at most three operations active, and return every permit even on a handled failure.
checks: Runtime checks cover twenty-four operations, one injected failure, peak active work, and returned permits. A separate source-order regression rejects moving acquisition inside either worker; it is not inferred from the active-work counter.
gsharpNotes: Await SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync before go so admission does not block a thread. finally returns the permit and scope joins the admitted work.
goNotes: A buffered channel acts as the semaphore. defer releases admission and WaitGroup.Go tracks completion.
limits: Neither example promises fairness or an admission deadline. Expected work failures are counted as results rather than silently discarded.

title: Cancellable pipeline
contract: Stages own and close their outputs. A consumer can stop early without leaving a producer or transformer blocked.
checks: Empty input, full delivery of eight values, early stop after three of one hundred values, and both stage finalizers observed.
gsharpNotes: Scoped channel operations observe the context. The published-SDK example explicitly normalizes expected OperationCanceledException when that context was cancelled.
goNotes: Context cancellation is selected alongside channel operations at both stages; the caller cancels and then joins.
limits: Cancellation remains cooperative. A CPU loop or unrelated blocking API does not become cancellable merely because it sits in a scope or goroutine.

title: Fan-in merge
contract: Forward multiple independently closed inputs into one output, closing the output only after all forwarders finish.
checks: Zero inputs and three producers; all fifteen values are unique and accounted for, including zero.
gsharpNotes: A nested scope makes the bounded topology explicit. The SDK also provides merge[T], checked here with empty and nonempty inputs; its full-channel inputs and unbounded output differ from this bounded, directional forwarding example.
goNotes: WaitGroup.Go tracks the forwarders and producers; a separate closer waits before closing the merged stream.
limits: Cross-input ordering is unspecified. This finite-stream example does not add early-consumer cancellation; use the pipeline protocol when that is required.

title: TTL cache with reader/writer locking
contract: Reads and writes synchronize access, and an entry is unavailable exactly at its expiry boundary.
checks: A missing key, a hit immediately before expiry, a miss at expiry, expiry-overflow rejection, and forty concurrent key-specific round trips using a controlled clock.
gsharpNotes: ReaderWriterLockSlim supplies the lock; defer releases it and a nullable string communicates a miss.
goNotes: RWMutex and a value/present pair provide the corresponding contract.
limits: The injected clock must suit elapsed-time decisions. ReaderWriterLockSlim is thread-affine: do not add await or channel operations while it is held; Get and Set are synchronous here. TTL controls visibility, not eviction, so expired keys remain allocated until overwritten or removed.

title: Keyed token-bucket rate limiting
contract: Each key has an independent bounded token balance; refill and admission are atomic under concurrent calls.
checks: Initial burst, fractional-time carry, refill boundary, independent keys, capacity cap, concurrent admission, and rejection of a backwards clock.
gsharpNotes: A lock and Dictionary implement the state transition; ordinary .NET synchronization is sufficient.
goNotes: A mutex and map express the same transition with explicit integer tick arithmetic.
limits: This is a discrete integer-token example, not a production policy library. Both use one global lock and retain keys; fairness, eviction, and distributed coordination are separate requirements.

title: Structured-concurrency All
contract: Wait for owned work, preserve a real failure, cancel cooperative siblings, and do not return while the blocked sibling is still active.
checks: Empty and successful scopes, a barrier-controlled failure with a blocked sibling whose finalizer must run, and unrequested cancellation while the parent is not cancelled.
gsharpNotes: Normal use is scope with go calls; the barriers and counters shown here are verification scaffolding. ScopeException carries failures, and the example normalizes cancellation using the context state.
goNotes: The self-contained standard-library runner combines Context, error returns, and WaitGroup.Go. A library such as errgroup is another idiomatic option.
limits: Go errors and panics are not CLR exceptions, and this runner does not recover panics. Both normalization policies use error category plus current context state, not cancellation provenance: an independent cancellation concurrent with group cancellation can be normalized. Failure ordering is not promised.

title: Timeout wrapper
contract: Distinguish ready work, a deadline, and explicit cancellation, and join a cooperative operation after stopping it.
checks: An already-ready result, an owned timer with no competing result, explicit cancellation, worker cleanup, and a Context.WithTimeout-backed .NET task; no tight latency assertion.
gsharpNotes: after and case cancelled integrate with select; using let owns the timer and scope supplies the join. Context.WithTimeout is also checked as an alternative for APIs accepting a .NET cancellation token.
goNotes: Timers and Context deadlines integrate with select; the example explicitly stops timers/cancels contexts and waits for the worker.
limits: A timeout does not guarantee arbitrary work has stopped. after starts a one-shot timer that remains armed until it fires or is disposed; losing-select deregistration alone does not stop it. Cleanup may exceed the deadline, and multiple ready select arms do not establish priority.

title: Channel ownership and routing
contract: A producer owns sending and closure; the consumer receives through a read-only handle and distinguishes closed state from a legitimate zero value.
checks: Empty and nonempty streams, zero as data, a closed two-value receive, and negative compilation checks for sending through a receive-only handle.
gsharpNotes: in chan[T] and out chan[T] expose capabilities in signatures; channel iteration and the ok flag avoid a nil/zero sentinel protocol.
goNotes: The directional <-chan and chan<- types offer the corresponding capability split and closed-receive check.
limits: Directional handles are not a linear ownership proof. The application must still choose one closer and define multi-writer coordination.

title: Atomic counter and lazy initialization
contract: Concurrent increments are not lost, and the lazy factory runs once while every caller observes the initialized value.
checks: No eager initialization, forty concurrent users, exact final count, one factory invocation, and a repeated read.
gsharpNotes: Interlocked and Lazy[T] with ExecutionAndPublication are .NET library tools, not special G# syntax.
goNotes: Typed atomic values and sync.OnceValue supply the corresponding successful-initialization behavior.
limits: An atomic field does not make a compound object invariant atomic. Factory failure/retry policies differ and are outside this successful-factory example.
